item.title: narratorAI
item.description:
## The Problem
Automated camera capture is easy; making sense of what was captured is not. This repo solves the narrow problem of turning periodic webcam snapshots into a spoken, character-voiced narration of whatever the camera sees. It is a demo of a three-stage pipeline: capture an image, describe it with a vision model, and read the description aloud with a synthetic voice.

item.title: Awesome AI Agents for Healthcare
item.description:
## The Problem
Agentic AI research in healthcare is published across venues and fragmented by modality (radiology, genomics, EHR), application (drug discovery, patient dialogue), and year. A clinician or researcher trying to track the field has no single index. This repo is that index: a curated, categorized list of papers, plus a survey paper and two data-visualization figures summarizing the literature landscape.

item.title: ekphos
item.description:
## The Problem
Researchers and writers who work in markdown need a tool that links notes, manages a knowledge graph, and supports vim-style editing without leaving the terminal. Obsidian does this in a GUI; Ekphos brings the same workflow to a TUI with a fraction of the resource footprint.
## What This Does
Ekphos is a Rust terminal application that renders markdown notes with an internal wiki-link graph, inline image support (iTerm2/Kitty/WezTerm/Sixel), vim modal editing, and themeable UI. ...

item.title: neural os
item.description:
## The Problem Training agents to interact with a real operating system is slow, serial, and hard to parallelize: every rollout needs a live desktop, and failures are expensive. NeuralOS replaces the OS with a neural model that predicts the next screen frame from mouse, click, and keyboard events, so policies can be trained and evaluated against a GPU-resident, differentiable environment instead of a physical machine.

item.title: flux2.c
item.description:
## The Problem
FLUX.2-class image generation normally requires a Python ML stack, a CUDA or MPS runtime, and roughly 16GB of RAM. That rules out headless servers, low-memory VMs, and Apple Silicon machines without a working PyTorch install.
